subject: Roundup: 'excluded damages' language — commercial compromise options
messages:
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
To: Dana Ross <dana.ross@acme.com>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 19 Mar 2028 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Excluded damages — commercial ask + redline

Dana — thanks for sending the order form. Attached is our internal read of Acme's proposed damages carve-out. High level: Acme is pushing a one-way consequential exclusion (Customer can't recover consequential/special/incidental/punitive from Acme) and wants no carveouts beyond willful misconduct/intent. That creates two problems for us: 1) commercial asymmetry for product outages/data incidents, and 2) precedent for other enterprise deals.

Can Neha/Karthik weigh in with legal's preferred approach and a prioritized list of tradeoffs we can offer? My preference (commercially) is a mutual exclusion with a short list of carveouts for: breach of confidentiality, data breach leading to regulatory fines, bodily injury, and indemnity claims. We can keep a single overall cap but adjust language so Acme can't use a broad one-way exclusion to avoid responsibility for security failures.

Attachment: acme-orderform-redline.docx (redline)

Next steps I propose: 
- Legal to propose 2 candidate redlines (mutual + compromise one-way w/ carveouts)
- Commercial to prioritize which carveouts we're flexible on (if any)
- If we can agree on carveouts, offer to accept Acme's one-way language in exchange for a higher cap for Acme's liability (or reciprocal language where feasible)

Thanks — S.

--

Date: Mon, 19 Mar 2028 11:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Excluded damages — commercial ask + redline

Stephanie — thanks. To be clear from our side: Acme's commercial team is focused on limiting vendor exposure for downstream consequential losses tied to our supply chain. We proposed the one-way exclusion so that Acme is not exposed if an upstream vendor (or customer) experiences a ripple effect. Our commercial counsel prefers a clean, one-way carveout with only the usual exceptions (willful misconduct, gross negligence).

Proposed snippet (from Acme counsel):
"Neither party shall be liable to the other for consequential, incidental, special, punitive, or exemplary damages arising out of or related to this Agreement, whether in contract, tort (including negligence), strict liability or otherwise, even if such party has been advised of the possibility of such damages. This limitation shall not apply to: (a) damages resulting from a party's gross negligence or willful misconduct; (b) obligations of indemnity; or (c) damages for bodily injury or death."

If Redwood can accept that text, we can move forward quickly. If not, let us know the precise carveouts you require so we can evaluate with our counsel.

Best,
Dana

Subject: Re: Excluded damages — commercial ask + redline (legal analysis and proposed compromise)

Stephanie / team — thanks for the ping and the attachments. Below is a short legal analysis and a recommended commercial compromise you can take back to Acme.

Summary position (short): we should not accept an unlimited one-way exclusion without carveouts. Commercially acceptable compromise: accept mutual exclusion of consequential/special/incidental/punitive damages, subject to an explicit list of carveouts tied to core risk areas (confidentiality/data breach leading to regulatory liability, indemnity, breach of payment obligations, bodily injury/death, and claims arising from gross negligence or willful misconduct). Keep overall aggregate cap (e.g., fees paid in prior 12 months) in place.

Rationale: 
- One-way exclusions give Acme asymmetric protection and allow them to disclaim responsibility for outages or data incidents that could materially damage our customers, which would harm Redwood's reputation and downstream exposure.
- Enumerated carveouts (especially for data breach/regulatory fines and indemnity) are standard and defensible; they align with our SOC 2 assurances and customer promises.
- Keeping the exclusion mutual preserves simplicity in commercial negotiations while protecting critical exposures.

Suggested compromise redline (short snippet you can send back):
"Neither party shall be liable to the other for consequential, incidental, special, punitive, or exemplary damages arising out of or related to this Agreement, whether in contract, tort (including negligence), strict liability or otherwise, even if such party has been advised of the possibility of such damages. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the limitation set forth in this paragraph shall not apply to: (i) a party's liability for damages resulting from that party's gross negligence or willful misconduct; (ii) damages resulting from a party's breach of confidentiality obligations or unauthorized disclosure of Customer Data; (iii) amounts payable under the indemnification provisions of this Agreement; (iv) damages resulting from bodily injury or death; and (v) statutory regulatory fines and penalties directly caused by a party's breach."

If Acme insists on one-way language, consider these negotiating levers: 
- Require a reciprocal cap increase (e.g., 2x) or a carveout for data/regulatory losses despite one-way language.
- Limit the temporal scope (e.g., exclude consequential damages only for third-party supply-chain claims but not for direct customer data incidents).
- Add a short-side letter or SOW amendment carving back liability for security incidents.

Action items for commercial: 
- Stephanie: present the mutual redline above as Redwood's preferred position; if Acme pushes back, offer the one-way option only with the enumerated carvebacks or an increased cap.
- Karthik: finalize the exact aggregate cap language we plan to live with (recommendation: fees paid in prior 12 months, 12-month lookback).
- Laura: confirm whether Finance will accept the increased cap trade for faster signature.

I can draft the redline email to Acme if you want — say so and I'll send the text directly to Dana and Acme Legal.

Neha Kapoor
